claims.text: The identity of X in CrFeCoNiX controls lattice mismatch at the metal/oxide interface.
The identity of X in CrFeCoNiX controls thermal-expansion mismatch at the metal/oxide interface.
Al or Si additions promote slowly growing, coherent protective oxide layers that remain adherent above 900 °C.
Mn does not promote an oxide phase sufficiently compatible with the alloy substrate.
Mn-containing CrFeCoNiX alloys form unstable oxides prone to cracking and spallation.
Arc melting followed by homogenization produces a uniform solid-solution microstructure in the proposed alloys.
Al-, Si-, and Mn-containing alloys should be compared while keeping the remaining composition and processing parameters constant.
Oxidation at approximately 950 °C for 100 hours in synthetic air or controlled oxygen is an intended simulation of the relevant service conditions.
Good lattice matching at the metal/oxide interface minimizes interfacial stress.
Good thermal-expansion matching at the metal/oxide interface minimizes interfacial stress.
Reduced interfacial stress makes the oxide layer coherent and slow-growing.
Al or Si changes the crystallographic and thermal compatibility between the forming oxide and the alloy substrate.
The relevant Al- or Si-containing oxide may be Al2O3 or a silica-rich mixed oxide.
Improved oxide/substrate compatibility reduces mismatch strain during thermal cycling and oxidation.
Reduced mismatch strain slows oxide growth and prevents stress accumulation that would otherwise initiate cracks and spallation.
Under identical exposure conditions, Al- or Si-containing alloys will exhibit more coherent, adherent, and slow-growing oxides than the Mn-containing alloy.
The proposed mechanism applies to high-temperature oxidative or corrosive atmospheres above 900 °C.
A lack of significant improvement in oxide coherence, adhesion, and growth behavior for Al or Si relative to Mn under identical conditions would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial-state field includes both single- and multiphase solid-solution states, whereas the boundary limits applicability to a homogeneous solid-solution state, leaving the inclusion of multiphase alloys internally inconsistent.
